title: Metric Markov cotype two of ℓ₁
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) that the sequence space l_1 has metric Markov cotype two, with the constant 12 sqrt 21. Metric Markov cotype two asks: given points of a metric space on the states of a reversible Markov chain and a time t, can the points be moved so that the cost of moving plus t times the one-step energy of the new points is at most a constant times the energy of the old points averaged over the times 1 to t. The first lesson gives the definition, proves the property for Hilbert space with averages along the chain, and compares averages over the times 1 to t with averages over a geometric random time. The second lesson represents finitely many points of l_1 by vertices of a weighted cube and proves an inequality for the cubic 3r^2 - 2r^3 applied in every coordinate. The third lesson proves the theorem; the new points are means of coordinatewise medians of three independent copies of the place where a randomly stopped walk ends. The fourth lesson treats complex scalars and the spaces L_1(mu), proves that Hilbert space has Markov type two and that l_1 is the dual of c_0, and derives the extension of Lipschitz maps from subsets of Hilbert space into l_1 from one named hypothesis, the extension theorem of Mendel and Naor.
prerequisites: finite sums, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, geometric series
core course Linear Algebra (B40): the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices (first lesson, Section 3; fourth lesson, Section 3)
core course Measure and Integration (D10): integrable functions (fourth lesson, Section 2 only)
core course Functional Analysis (D20): normed spaces and bounded linear functionals (fourth lesson, Section 4 only)
the lessons prove every other fact they use, except the named hypothesis (MN) of the fourth lesson

checks.reading: The manuscript 'Metric Markov Cotype Two of l_1' (OpenAI, 5 Oct 2026, in the revision of the repository on 13 Oct 2026; six sections, 648 lines of TeX) was read in full on 13 Oct 2026, and every step of its argument was derived again while the lessons were written: the cut representation (the nested cuts of one coordinate, the reconstruction identity, the distance identities, the contraction); the bound for the derivative of the cubic; the increment bound 6|a||delta| + 3|delta|^2; the exact identity for the remainder of the fourth power; the constants 72, 18, 36 + 72 = 108; the vanishing of the linear term by the first-step identity; the identity q/p = t; the subadditivity of the square roots of the energies; the second moment 2t^2 + t of the geometric time; q^t <= 1/2; the constants 2*3*4 + 2*2 = 28 and 108*28 = 3024 = 144*21; the median description; the complex case. No error found. Differences of presentation, none a correction: the energy inequality is proved with finite sums and one geometric series (a one-state inequality, applied along the powers of the matrix, telescoped and averaged over the start) in place of a martingale with a limit; the comparison of the two averages is written with sums in place of a random time; the main theorem is stated for stationary matrices from the start (the manuscript notes this in a remark). Additions that are not in the manuscript, each proved in the lessons: Hilbert space has metric Markov cotype two with C^2 = 5 by Cesaro averages; the theorem for L_1(mu) of an arbitrary measure space with the same constant; the lower bound N_2 >= 1/sqrt 5 for every space with two points; Markov type two of Hilbert space with the constant 1 and the duality of l_1 with c_0 (both quoted in the manuscript); the sharper form of the energy inequality with the initial potential is the manuscript's first inequality. The extension theorem of Mendel and Naor (arXiv:1301.3963v2) was fetched and its statements (Definitions 1.1 to 1.3, Theorem 1.11, Corollary 1.13, Question 1.15, Theorem 1.14) were read on 13 Oct 2026; its proof was not read. Checked by the program plan/checks_20261013/mc_check.py (seven parts, exact rational arithmetic: the flat inequality on 4,000 random pairs; the cut representation on 387 random point sets; the geometric sums and the comparison of the averages on 300 random chains, reversible, only stationary, and with a state of stationary weight 0; the whole construction on 238 random instances and on cycles, with the first-step identity, the one-state inequality for every centre, both intermediate inequalities, the final inequality and the mean-of-medians formula exactly; the Hilbert space statements on 200 random chains and the scalar inequality for t <= 80; the examples of the lessons; weighted coordinates). All parts pass on the first run (output mc_check_run_20261013.txt; the program was run a second time after its printed precision was raised). The statements about the history (Ball's question; the condition with linear averages that fails in l_1; the subspace of l_1 without the property) are quoted from the manuscript and from Mendel and Naor and were not checked.

open_obligations: Named hypothesis (MN), the extension theorem of Mendel and Naor (arXiv:1301.3963, Theorem 1.11 with Corollary 1.13): for a metric space of Markov type two and a dual Banach space of metric Markov cotype two, Lipschitz maps from subsets extend with a constant bounded by a universal multiple of the product of the two constants. It is not proved in the programme. Only Corollary 5.1 of the fourth lesson (extension from Hilbert space into l_1) depends on it; the cotype theorem and all other statements do not.

The spectral theorem for symmetric matrices (core course Linear Algebra, B40), the basic properties of integrable functions (core course Measure and Integration, D10) and of bounded linear functionals (core course Functional Analysis, D20) are taken from the core courses; the exact locators in their texts have not been looked up.

Not in the course: the best constant; whether L_1(mu) admits the extension of Lipschitz maps from Hilbert space (it is in general not a dual space); the extension statement for complex scalars; the equivalence of the definition with Ball's original metric definition.
The history of the question is not told beyond two sentences and was not checked.
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
